practice.intro: Play the strings one by one. I recognize them in any order.
practice.doneMessage: Every string sounds as it should. Repeat it slowly until it comes naturally.
practice.tipSoundsOpen: The $string rings open: press fret $fret with $finger.

tipMoveUp.one: It sounds lower. Move $finger up one fret toward the body.
tipMoveUp.other: It sounds lower. Move $finger up $n frets toward the body.

tipMoveDown.one: It sounds higher. Move $finger down one fret toward the headstock.
tipMoveDown.other: It sounds higher. Move $finger down $n frets toward the headstock.

practice.tipTooFlat: It sounds a bit flat. Bring $finger closer to the fret (without touching it) or retune the string.
practice.tipTooSharp: It sounds a bit sharp. Press more lightly, without bending the string, or retune it.
practice.tipRetuneUp: The open $string sounds flat: tighten the peg a little.
practice.tipRetuneDown: The open $string sounds sharp: loosen the peg a little.
practice.tipUnknown: I don't recognize that note. Play only the $string, calmly.

howTo(map).guessNote: You will hear a single guitar note. Pick its name. Easy has natural notes only; hard has all twelve.
howTo(map).whichString: You will hear an open string. Say which one it is, from 6th (the lowest) to 1st (the highest). Easy has only three.
howTo(map).whichFret: You will hear the open string and then the same string fretted. Each fret rises one semitone: count how many.
howTo(map).interval: You will hear two notes in a row, low to high. Recognise the distance between them: third, fifth, octave…
howTo(map).higherLower: You will hear two notes. Say whether the first or the second sounds higher. On hard they are almost the same.
howTo(map).chordQuality: You will hear a chord. Tell whether it is major (bright), minor (sad), seventh and more as you level up.
howTo(map).nameChord: You will hear a chord from the bank. Pick its name among several similar options.
howTo(map).tuneEar: You will hear a reference note and another that may be flat, in tune or sharp. Train your tuner ear.
howTo(map).memory: You will hear a sequence of open strings. Tap them in the same order. Each question adds more notes.
howTo(map).noteAtFret: You get a string and a fret. Say which note it is. You will learn the fretboard without looking at the guitar.
howTo(map).fretOfNote: You get a string and a note. Say which fret it is on (0 is the open string).
howTo(map).fingerQuiz: You will see a chord with one string marked and no numbers. Say which finger presses it: 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 pinky.
howTo(map).readDiagram: You will see the diagram of a position. Recognise which chord it is.
howTo(map).buildChord: You get the name of a chord. Place your fingers on the fretboard and check. Then play it on your guitar.
howTo(map).playNote: You are asked for a note. Play it on any string: the microphone recognises it. You can hear the note first.
howTo(map).playStringFret: You are asked for an exact string and fret. Press and play: the microphone checks that the right note sounds.
howTo(map).echo: You will hear a short melody. Play it on your guitar note by note, in the same order.
howTo(map).scaleNote: A scale and its tonic are shown. Pick the only option that belongs to that scale. Use the formula or picture the box on the neck.
howTo(map).keyChord: A key and a degree in Roman numerals are shown. Pick the chord on that degree. Remember: in major, I IV V are major; ii iii vi are minor.
howTo(map).scaleDegree: A key and a note are shown. Say which degree it is (I = tonic, IV = subdominant, V = dominant…).
howTo(map).findTonic: A four-chord cadence plays and ends at home. Pick the note that sounds like rest: the tonic.
howTo(map).progressionEar: Four chords play. Pick which progression it is, written in degrees. Notice whether it starts major or minor and how it gets back home.

scaleAbout(map).major: The foundation of harmony: happy and stable. Pop, folk and children's songs.
scaleAbout(map).minor: The major's relative: melancholic and epic. Ballads, rock and metal.
scaleAbout(map).harmonicMinor: Minor with a raised seventh: classical, flamenco and neoclassical flavor.
scaleAbout(map).minorPentatonic: Five notes that never fail: the heart of rock and blues.
scaleAbout(map).majorPentatonic: Sweet and open: country, pop, soul and melodic solos.
scaleAbout(map).blues: Minor pentatonic plus the blue note (b5): pure attitude.
scaleAbout(map).dorian: Minor with a major sixth: funk, jazz, Santana and Pink Floyd.
scaleAbout(map).phrygian: Minor with a minor second: flamenco and dark metal.
scaleAbout(map).lydian: Major with a raised fourth: dreamy, soundtrack-like.
scaleAbout(map).mixolydian: Major with a minor seventh: classic rock, blues and country.

strumAbout(map).whole: A single downstroke at the start of the bar; let the chord ring. Ideal for changing chords calmly.
strumAbout(map).quarters: A downstroke on every beat (1, 2, 3 and 4). Simple and steady: the best way to start.
strumAbout(map).pop: The universal strum: ↓ ↓↑ ↑↓↑. Your arm never stops moving; you just skip a few hits.
strumAbout(map).eighths: Steady eighths ↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑ accenting the beats: the energy of rock.
strumAbout(map).boomChick: Bass on 1 and 3 and a strum on 2 and 4: "boom-chick". Alternate root and fifth in the bass.
strumAbout(map).skank: Silence on the beats and a dry hit only on the offbeat.
strumAbout(map).bossa: Thumb on the bass and syncopated chords with the fingers: the soft sway of bossa nova.
strumAbout(map).shuffle: Long-short on every beat, like a triplet without the middle note: the sway of the blues.
strumAbout(map).waltz: In 3/4: bass on 1 and two light strums on 2 and 3, "one-two-three".
strumAbout(map).cumbia: Bass on 1 and 3 and a short ↓↑ strum on the offbeat: "boom-chiki, boom-chiki".
strumAbout(map).salsa: Syncopated hits leaning on the "and" of the beats, leaving room for the bass and the clave.
strumAbout(map).reggaeton: The dembow: hits on 1, the "and" of 2, 3 and 4. It demands a very steady pulse.
strumAbout(map).rumba: Down, down-up, a dry tap on the top (✕), up and down-up: the hallmark of the flamenco rumba.
strumAbout(map).ska: Only very short upstrokes on every offbeat: ·↑·↑·↑·↑.
strumAbout(map).disco: A strong hit on every beat with the offbeat muted (✕), like the "four on the floor" kick.
strumAbout(map).bolero: Bass on 1 and chords falling between the beats with a soft syncopation.
strumAbout(map).tango: Marcato: firm, dry hits on the beats, a muted hit (✕) and a ↑ push at the end.
strumAbout(map).valsRanchero: In 3/4: bass on 1, chord on 2 and a ↓↑ bounce on 3 that pushes into the next bar.
strumAbout(map).valsCriollo: In 3/4: bass on 1 and a dragged ↓↑↓ chord leaning toward the third beat.
strumAbout(map).merengue: A constant pulse with the hand tuned to the offbeat, quick and cheerful.
strumAbout(map).bachata: Bass on 1 and linked ↓↑ hits accenting 2 and 4.
strumAbout(map).campfire: ↓ ↓ ↓↑ ↓↑: the strum heard around every campfire. Easy and wide open.
strumAbout(map).funkMuted: Dry hits (✕) dragging between open chords: the hand never stops moving.
strumAbout(map).arpeggio: Bass and single notes going up and down, softly: ideal for ballads.
strumAbout(map).downstrokes: Eighths always downward: the speed and drive of punk and grunge.
strumAbout(map).gallop: An eighth and two sixteenths, all down: the metal gallop, palm-muted.
strumAbout(map).lofi: Lazy, dragging chords: ↓ ·· ↑ ↓ · ↑. Let the gaps breathe.
strumAbout(map).charleston: A chord on 1 and on the "and" of 2: the rhythm of pre-swing jazz.
strumAbout(map).trainBeat: Bass and two quick ↓↓ hits in each half of the bar: the country "chug-a-chug" train.
strumAbout(map).tresillo: 3+3+2: hits on 1, the "and" of 2 and 4; the rhythm of habanera and milonga.
strumAbout(map).rockBallad: Two firm hits and a ↓↑↓ push into the next bar: the rock ballad.

genreAbout(map).cumbia: Born on Colombia's Caribbean coast and adopted across Latin America. Simple chords (i–iv–V7), a marked bass on 1 and 3 and the "chiqui" strum on the offbeat. Very danceable and easy to learn.
genreAbout(map).salsa: Caribbean and New York music built on clave, horns and percussion. The guitar rarely leads: it plays montunos and syncopated chords (I–IV–V7, ii–V–I) that talk to the bass and the clave.
genreAbout(map).ranchera: Mexican popular song with mariachi, guitar and guitarrón. It works as a waltz (3/4), polka, corrido or bolero, with major chords, the dominant seventh and a lot of feeling in the singing.
genreAbout(map).flamenco: Gypsy-Andalusian music built on the phrygian cadence (Am–G–F–E) and the phrygian scale. The guitar backs singing and dance in 12-beat or 4/4 compás (rumba, tangos), with fan strums and taps on the top.
genreAbout(map).bolero: Cuban and Mexican romance: slow tempo and sighing chords (I–vi–ii–V7, i–VI–iv–V7). Played with guitar and requinto, with a soft syncopation in the picking hand.
genreAbout(map).tango: Music from the River Plate born in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Minor harmony with very dramatic dominants (V7), bandoneon, violin and piano. The guitar marks the beat firmly.
genreAbout(map).ska: Pre-reggae Jamaica, faster and happier. The guitar plays short upstrokes on every offbeat while the bass walks. Its later waves (two-tone, third wave) blend it with punk.
genreAbout(map).indie: Bright guitars, open chords with suspended 2nds and 4ths, arpeggios and pop progressions. Intimate yet polished, with layered guitars and lots of texture.
genreAbout(map).grunge: Seattle, 1990s: dirty distorted guitars, power chords and a strong contrast between quiet verses and huge choruses. A blend of punk, metal and pop with gloomy lyrics.
genreAbout(map).disco: Seventies dance floor: octave bass, "four on the floor" drums, strings and a guitar chopping the offbeat with short chords (m7, 9, maj7).
genreAbout(map).reggaeton: Born in Panama and Puerto Rico out of Spanish-language reggae and the dembow. A heavily marked drum pattern, minor chords on loop and catchy melodies.
genreAbout(map).lofi: Mellow beats for studying or relaxing: maj7 and m7 chords with a jazzy flavor, a lazy pulse and a slightly "worn" sound. The guitar repeats a short progression very calmly.
genreAbout(map).pop: Catchy songs over a few progressions (I-V-vi-IV). The guitar backs them with open chords and a steady strum.
genreAbout(map).rock: Power chords, driving eighth notes and minor pentatonic riffs. I-IV-V and the bVII rule.
genreAbout(map).blues: Twelve bars, seventh chords and the blues scale. Feel matters more than speed.
genreAbout(map).country: Open chords, alternating bass and major pentatonic melodies. Simple stories and lots of swing in the picking hand.
genreAbout(map).jazz: Seventh chords (maj7, m7, 7), the ii-V-I and constant key changes. Played light and swinging.
genreAbout(map).funk: Ninth and m7 chords played short and percussive. The guitar is part of the drum kit.
genreAbout(map).ballad: Slow tempos and chords left ringing. Arpeggios or one strum per beat.
genreAbout(map).latin: From the ranchera in 3/4 to the Andalusian cadence and bolero. Lots of harmonic minor.
genreAbout(map).reggae: The chord only sounds on the offbeats, short and dry. Bass and drums carry the beat.
genreAbout(map).bossa: Soft seventh chords, thumb bass and syncopated chords with the fingers.
genreAbout(map).metal: Palm-muted power chords, fast tempos and minor, phrygian and harmonic scales.
genreAbout(map).punk: Three or four power chords, downstroked eighths and lots of speed. Attitude first.
genreAbout(map).soul: Color chords (maj7, m7, 9), a relaxed groove and major pentatonic fills.
genreAbout(map).gospel: Church harmony: I-IV-V with sevenths, the minor iv and plagal ('amen') cadences.
genreAbout(map).folk: Timeless songs with three or four open chords. Perfect for singing along.

genreRhythm(map).cumbia: Bass on 1 and 3 and a short ↓↑ strum on the offbeat: 'boom-chiki, boom-chiki'.
genreRhythm(map).salsa: Syncopated chords landing on the "and" of the beats, leaving room for the bass (tumbao) and the 3-2 or 2-3 clave. Often just the top strings.
genreRhythm(map).ranchera: In waltz time: bass on 1, chord on 2 and a ↓↑ bounce on 3. In polka or corrido the bass and strum alternate (boom-chick).
genreRhythm(map).flamenco: Flamenco rumba: down, down-up, a dry tap on the top (✕), up and down-up. Each chord is struck hard with precise silences.
genreRhythm(map).bolero: Bass on 1 and chords falling between the beats for a soft syncopation: boom – cha-ka – cha-ka. Slow and heartfelt.
genreRhythm(map).tango: Marcato: firm, dry hits on every beat with an occasional muted hit (✕) and a final ↑ leading into the next bar.
genreRhythm(map).ska: A very short upstroke on every offbeat (the "and" of each beat) with the bass walking on the beats.
genreRhythm(map).indie: Campfire strum (↓ ↓ ↓↑ ↓↑) with a soft pick, alternating with arpeggios that let the open strings ring.
genreRhythm(map).grunge: Eighths all downstrokes on power chords; loose in the verse and with hard accents in the chorus.
genreRhythm(map).disco: A strong hit on every beat with the offbeat muted (↓ ✕ ↓↑): a steady groove around 120 bpm.
genreRhythm(map).reggaeton: The "dembow": hits on 1, the "and" of 2, 3 and 4. The strum leans on those accents and leaves silences between them.
genreRhythm(map).lofi: Long, dragging chords with a lazy rhythm (↓ ·· ↑ ↓ · ↑); leave gaps so it can breathe.
genreRhythm(map).rock: Down or down-up eighths, palm-muted in the verses.
genreRhythm(map).country: Boom-chick: bass on 1 and 3, strum on 2 and 4, alternating the bass string.
genreRhythm(map).jazz: Four short strums per bar (Freddie Green style), swinging.
genreRhythm(map).funk: Sixteenths with the hand always moving; mostly muted with a few open hits.
genreRhythm(map).ballad: One strum per bar or a slow arpeggio from the 6th to the 1st string.
genreRhythm(map).latin: Ranchera: bass-chord-chord (3/4). Rumba: strum accenting the offbeat.
genreRhythm(map).reggae: Silence on 1, a dry hit on 2 and 4 (skank).
genreRhythm(map).bossa: Thumb on the bass every beat and a syncopated chord in between.
genreRhythm(map).metal: Eighths or gallop (an eighth and two sixteenths), palm-muted.
genreRhythm(map).soul: Soft hits on 2 and 4 with fills between chords.
genreRhythm(map).gospel: Firm quarter notes accenting 2 and 4; call and response.
genreRhythm(map).folk: Quarters or the pop pattern; in 3/4, bass plus two strums.

genreTip(map).cumbia: Mute the strings with your palm between hits for a dry "chiqui", and start with just Am, Dm and E7.
genreTip(map).salsa: Learn a two-chord montuno (C6–A7), let the bass mark beat 1 and listen to the clave before you play.
genreTip(map).ranchera: Alternate the bass between the root and fifth of the chord and never forget the V7 that returns to I: it is the ranchera hallmark.
genreTip(map).flamenco: Start with the Andalusian cadence in A minor and strum everything with one pattern before adding ornaments; a capo changes key without changing shapes.
genreTip(map).bolero: Play the bass with your thumb (root and fifth) and the syncopated chord with the other fingers; the softer, the better.
genreTip(map).tango: Practice the V7 → i phrase ending and stop your hand for an instant before changing: silence is tango too.
genreTip(map).ska: Strum only the top three strings with a relaxed hand and mute them at once; practice with a metronome at 120 before speeding up.
genreTip(map).indie: Try chords with open strings (Dsus2, Asus4, Gsus2) and let them ring; one guitar holds the rhythm while another plays a melodic line over it.
genreTip(map).grunge: Play with contrast: a muted, sparse verse and open, full-arm strokes in the chorus.
genreTip(map).disco: Mute the strings with your fretting hand right after each hit; the cleanness of the cut is the groove.
genreTip(map).reggaeton: With only four chords (Am–F–C–G) a rock-steady pulse is what matters; the guitar often doubles the synth line.
genreTip(map).lofi: Play the chords on four strings, let them ring and add a pentatonic fill every four bars, no more.
genreTip(map).pop: Learn I-V-vi-IV in G, C and D: you'll play hundreds of songs.
genreTip(map).rock: Palm-mute the verses and let the chorus ring open.
genreTip(map).blues: Bend the 4th up to the 5th of the scale and end phrases on the tonic.
genreTip(map).country: Alternate the bass between the root and the fifth for the classic boom-chick.
genreTip(map).jazz: Learn m7, 7 and maj7 shapes rooted on the 6th and 5th strings: they cover 90%.
genreTip(map).funk: Strum close to the bridge and relax the fretting hand to mute between hits.
genreTip(map).ballad: Let chords ring and change right before beat 1, not late.
genreTip(map).latin: In the Andalusian cadence use harmonic minor over the V chord (E major in A minor).
genreTip(map).reggae: Play the skank on the top three strings and mute it right away.
genreTip(map).bossa: Practice the thumb bass alone before adding the chords.
genreTip(map).metal: Dial in the palm mute: hand on the bridge, not too far on or off.
genreTip(map).punk: Keep the wrist loose: speed comes from relaxation.
genreTip(map).soul: Play chords on the top three or four strings for a clean sound.
genreTip(map).gospel: Try IV → iv → I: the major-to-minor change is pure emotion.
genreTip(map).folk: Sing while you play: the strumming hand should run on autopilot.

lessonSummaries(map).caged: Five open chord shapes that cover the whole neck.

lessonBodies(map).intervalSongs:
An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in semitones (frets on the same string). Learning them from songs is the shortcut to recognizing them by ear: your memory already knows how each leap sounds.

Minor second (1 semitone): the "Jaws" theme. Major second (2): "Frère Jacques". Major third (4): the opening of "When the Saints Go Marching In". Perfect fourth (5): "Amazing Grace" (A-ma-zing) or the bridal march. Tritone (6): "Maria" from West Side Story and the Simpsons theme. Perfect fifth (7): "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" and the Star Wars theme. Major sixth (9): "My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean". Octave (12): "Somewhere over the Rainbow".

To practice, play the first interval on two strings and sing it before checking. On the guitar the same distance looks the same all over the neck, so every shape you learn can be moved.
lessonBodies(map).subdivision:
The beat can be divided in several ways. Quarter notes: one hit per beat ("1 2 3 4"). Eighths: two per beat ("1 and 2 and"), the engine of rock and pop: down on the beat, up on the "and". Sixteenths: four per beat ("1 e and a"), typical of funk. Triplets: three per beat ("1-trip-let"), the sway of slow blues, creole waltz and 6/8.

Syncopation means accenting where it is not expected: the offbeat (the "and") or leaving the beat silent. Reggae, ska and salsa live on it. Swing and shuffle are "uneven" eighths: the first lasts twice as long as the second (like the first and third notes of a triplet), which gives the sway.

Study trick: keep your arm moving constantly (down on the beat, up on the "and") and only change which hits you play and which you leave silent. That way the patterns in the genre guide come almost on their own.
lessonBodies(map).modesPractical:
In practice you choose a mode from the chord that is sounding, not from theory. Over a minor 7 chord (Em7) play dorian: the minor scale "with a major sixth", the recipe of funk, jazz and Santana. Over a dominant 7 (G7) or a rock major chord with a bVII, play mixolydian: major "with a flat seventh". Over a dreamy major chord (Fmaj7) play lydian: major with a raised fourth, cinematic. Over a minor chord with a bII (Em–F) play phrygian: the flavor of flamenco and metal.

Each mode is told apart by its characteristic note: the major 6th in dorian, the b2 in phrygian, the #4 in lydian and the b7 in mixolydian. Lean on that note, resolve it to the tonic and the mode will be heard at once.

Quick recipe: pick a one- or two-chord vamp, find the tonic on the 6th string and play the scale from there; use the scale explorer to see the positions in all 12 keys.
lessonBodies(map).triads:
A chord is built by stacking thirds above a note, the root. A major third is 4 semitones and a minor third 3. The major triad is root + major third + fifth (0-4-7, like C–E–G); the minor one swaps in a minor third (0-3-7: C–E♭–G). The diminished stacks two minor thirds (0-3-6) and the augmented two major ones (0-4-8).

Add another third on top and the sevenths appear: major 7 (0-4-7-11, dreamy), dominant 7 (0-4-7-10, tense and wanting to resolve), minor 7 (0-3-7-10, soft) and, on the diminished triad, the half-diminished (m7♭5), typical of the minor ii–V. The third is the note that decides whether a chord sounds happy or sad.

This way you can work out any chord without memorizing it: count the semitones from the root and look for those notes on the strings. In C major, stacking thirds on every scale note gives seven chords: three major, three minor and one diminished.
lessonBodies(map).extensions:
If you keep stacking thirds past the seventh you get the extensions: the ninth (9), the eleventh (11) and the thirteenth (13). They are notes 2, 4 and 6 an octave higher. A ninth chord (C9) is a dominant 7 with the ninth added: richer and funkier than C7. In practice not every note is played: the fifth is left out and, on dominants, the eleventh clashes with the third.

Suspended chords (sus) replace the third with another note: sus2 uses the second and sus4 the fourth. They are neither major nor minor; they sound open, in suspension, and sus4 usually resolves to the major chord (Dsus4 → D). Add chords add a note without the seventh: Cadd9 is a major triad with the ninth, bright and modern (very common in indie and pop).

What to use where: 9 in funk and soul, maj7 and m7 in jazz and lo-fi, sus2 and sus4 in pop and indie, 6 and m6 in bossa and bolero. Try swapping a chord in a progression for its colorful version and hear how the mood changes.
lessonBodies(map).inversions:
A chord does not always sound with its root in the bass. If the lowest note is the third it is in first inversion; if it is the fifth, in second inversion. It is written with a slash: C/E is a C with E in the bass, C/G a C with G. The note after the slash is always the bass note, and it can even be a non-chord note (C/D).

They do two jobs: they give the bass some movement and they smooth the changes. A descending line C – G/B – Am – Am/G – F – C/E – Dm – G (the "canon bass line") sounds fluid because the bass moves by step. On guitar, C/E is an open C played with the open 6th string too; G/B is a G with the B on the 5th string (fret 2) and D/F♯ puts the F♯ on the 6th string (fret 2).

In the Chords bank many chords have inversion shapes (movable triads with the root or the third in the bass). Look them up on the chord page and practice the C – G/B – Am link.
lessonBodies(map).circleFifths:
The circle of fifths lines up the 12 keys by fifths. Going right, each step adds a sharp: C (none), G (1), D (2), A (3), E (4), B (5), F♯ (6). Going left it adds a flat: F (1), B♭ (2), E♭ (3), A♭ (4). Inside each major key lives its relative minor (C–A minor, G–E minor…).

It is a map of kinship: two neighbors on the circle share six of seven notes, so modulating between them is smooth. And it gives you the chords of a key at a glance: the I (your key) with its two neighbors, the IV on the left and the V on the right. In G major, C (IV) and D (V) are its neighbors.

It also marks a very natural harmonic path: descending fifths. iii–vi–ii–V–I (Em–Am–Dm–G7–C) follows the circle to the left and sounds like a "resolution" at every step; it is the basis of jazz, rancheras and half of classic pop.
lessonBodies(map).cadences:
A cadence is the formula of two or more chords that ends a phrase, like punctuation. The authentic one (V–I, best with V7–I) is the full stop: the most conclusive, because the leading note rises to the tonic. The plagal (IV–I) is the gospel "amen" and sounds gentler and more solemn.

The half cadence ends on V (I–V, ii–V…): a comma, the phrase stays open and asks for more. The deceptive cadence (V–vi) fools the ear: you expect I and get vi, which sounds similar but sad, and extends the phrase. And the Andalusian cadence (i–♭VII–♭VI–V, Am–G–F–E) steps down to a major V: it is the cadence of flamenco, rumba and many rock and Latin pop songs.

Listen to them by feeling: has it ended? is something missing? did it surprise me? Learn to hear when a song "makes a comma" and when it "puts the full stop" and it will be much easier to accompany and anticipate the changes.
lessonBodies(map).relativeParallel:
The relative key shares the same notes but has a different tonic: C major and A minor use the same seven notes. The relative minor sits three semitones below the major tonic (or the major, three above the minor). That is why the same chords work in both: C, Dm, Em, F, G and Am belong to both C major and A minor; only which one sounds like "home" changes.

The parallel key shares the tonic but changes the mode: C major and C minor. Here the notes change (the 3rd, 6th and 7th drop a semitone) and so do the chords: C major has F, C minor has Fm.

That allows modal interchange: borrowing a chord from the parallel key for color. The IV–iv of gospel (F → Fm over C), the rock ♭VII (B♭ over C) or the epic ♭VI come from the parallel minor. When a song suddenly sounds "darker" it is often borrowing a chord.
lessonBodies(map).transposeCapo:
Transposing means moving a whole song to another key while keeping the degrees: every chord moves by the same number of semitones. It is done to fit the singer's voice or to use more comfortable shapes. In the Chords songbook you can transpose ±6 semitones with one tap.

The capo raises all the open strings by a semitone per fret: with the capo on fret 2, G shapes sound as A, C shapes as D and E shapes as F♯. The formula is: sounding key = shape + capo fret. If the song is in D and you want to play C shapes, put the capo on fret 2.

To choose: look at the chords in the original key, find a key where they can be played with open shapes (G, C, D, Em, Am) and work out the fret. The capo also gives a bright timbre and more open strings, widely used in folk and pop.
lessonBodies(map).styleComping:
A progression like I–V–vi–IV can be pop, reggae, ballad, indie or cumbia: what changes is how you play it. There are four ingredients. The strumming pattern (which hits you play and which you leave silent), the dynamics (soft in the verse, loud in the chorus), the register (low strings, high strings or all) and the muting (long chords or short, dry ones).

Examples: pop uses ↓ ↓↑ ↑↓↑; reggae stays silent on the beats and plays only on the offbeat; the ballad arpeggiates or strums once per bar; cumbia puts the bass on 1 and 3 and a "chiqui" on the offbeat; funk mutes almost everything and leaves a few hits; heavy rock uses palm-muted power chords. The genre guide gathers each style's pattern with its tempo.

Exercise: pick a jam progression and play the same loop in four different styles. If you change the pattern and the tempo, even the meaning of the song changes.
lessonBodies(map).tunings:
Standard tuning is E–A–D–G–B–E (EADGBE). Changing a string opens new sounds. In Drop D you lower just the 6th string a whole step (D–A–D–G–B–E): power chords are played with one finger across the three low strings and the low end sounds heavier; it is the tuning of grunge, metal and hard rock.

DADGAD (D–A–D–G–A–D) has no third in its open chords: it sounds open, neither major nor minor, which is why it is used in Celtic folk and fingerstyle. In open G (D–G–D–G–B–D) the open strings form a G major chord: with one finger or a slide you reach every chord; it is the tuning of Delta blues and slide rock.

Tips: tune string by string with the app's tuner, lower the pitch slowly (the neck adapts) and recheck the tuning after a while. When the tuning changes, the chords you know change shape: learn four or five shapes first and go back to standard when you finish.
lessonBodies(map).notes:
Western music uses only 12 notes that repeat in octaves: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯ and B.

Between two neighboring notes there is a half step, and on the guitar a half step is exactly one fret; two frets make a whole step. There is no sharp between E and F or between B and C: they are a half step apart.

A sharp (♯) raises a note a half step and a flat (♭) lowers it, so C♯ and D♭ are the same note with two names. At the 12th fret every string repeats its open note an octave higher: that's where the neck starts over.
lessonBodies(map).intervals:
An interval is the distance between two notes, measured in half steps (frets). Each distance has its own color: the major third (4 half steps) sounds happy, the minor third (3) sad and the perfect fifth (7) solid and open.

Chords are built by stacking intervals on a root: a major chord is root + major third + fifth; a minor chord only changes the third. That's why moving a single note one fret turns C into C minor.

On the guitar every interval has a shape: the fifth is on the next (higher) string, two frets up, and the octave two strings over and two frets up. When crossing the 2nd (B) string the shape shifts one fret.
lessonBodies(map).tonic:
The tonic is the note a song revolves around: the home everything wants to return to. When the melody or chord lands on the tonic we feel rest; moving away creates tension.

The key is the tonic plus its scale. 'G major' means G is home and the notes come from the G major scale. Almost every song ends, and many start, on the tonic chord.

To find a song's key, look for the chord that sounds like an ending, check that the other chords belong to that key and sing the note that 'closes' the melody. With practice you'll hear it instantly: play 'Find the tonic'.
lessonBodies(map).rhythm:
The beat is music's steady pulse. Meter groups beats: 4/4 (four per bar) is the meter of pop, rock and almost everything; 3/4 belongs to the waltz, the ranchera and many folk songs.

Each beat splits into two eighth notes: down on the beat ('1') and up on the offbeat ('and'). The strumming hand always moves down-up like a pendulum, even when it doesn't hit the strings: that way the rhythm never breaks.

Each genre has its pattern: pop (↓ ↓↑ ↑↓↑), rock (eighths), country (boom-chick), reggae (offbeats only) or blues (shuffle). Jam mode shows the pattern stroke by stroke while you play.
lessonBodies(map).majorScale:
The major scale has seven notes and always follows the same formula of whole (W) and half (H) steps: W W H W W W H. From C you get C D E F G A B, all natural notes.

With the formula you can build it from any note. From G: G A B C D E F♯; the F♯ appears to keep the last whole step before the final half step.

On a single string you play the major scale by counting frets: 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1. Try it on the 5th string from the 3rd fret (C) and hear the famous do-re-mi. The explorer shows its seven three-notes-per-string positions.
lessonBodies(map).minorScales:
The natural minor scale changes the formula: W H W W H W W. A minor uses the same notes as C major (A B C D E F G), but starting on A makes everything darker: it is C's relative minor.

Every major key has a relative minor three half steps below (G major ↔ E minor). They share notes and chords; only home changes.

The harmonic minor raises the seventh note a half step (G♯ in A minor). That note makes the fifth-degree chord major (E major in A minor), which pulls hard toward the tonic: the sound of flamenco, classical music and many boleros.
lessonBodies(map).pentatonic:
The pentatonic is a five-note scale: it drops the two most tense notes of the major or minor scale. That's why almost any note you play over the song's chords will sound good.

The minor pentatonic (1 b3 4 5 b7) is the backbone of rock and blues: A C D E G in A minor. The major pentatonic (1 2 3 5 6) sounds sweet and open, typical of country and pop: C D E G A in C.

Key trick: A minor pentatonic and C major pentatonic share the same notes. The same shape with a different tonic gives you both sounds. Lean on the major tonic to sound major, on the minor one to sound bluesy.
lessonBodies(map).positions:
A position or box is the group of scale notes you can reach without moving your hand: four or five frets, one finger per fret. The pentatonic has five boxes and seven-note scales have seven three-notes-per-string positions.

Boxes fit together like puzzle pieces: the right edge of one is the left edge of the next, and after the last one the first returns twelve frets higher. Knowing them all lets you play the scale across the whole neck.

Position 1 of the minor pentatonic starts with the tonic on the 6th string under the index finger. Learn it first, then 2, and connect them by sliding a finger. Changing key needs nothing new: move the whole box to the new tonic.
lessonBodies(map).blues:
The blues scale is the minor pentatonic plus one note: the flat fifth (b5), the famous blue note. In A: A C D D♯ E G. Use it in passing on the way to the fifth; don't sit on it.

The classic blues lasts 12 bars with three seventh chords: four bars of I7, two of IV7, two of I7, then V7, IV7, I7 and V7 to start over (the 'turnaround').

The rhythm is the shuffle: each beat splits into a long and a short hit (da-ga, da-ga). Try the '12-bar blues' jam and play the blues scale over it.
lessonBodies(map).modes:
If you play the notes of C major starting on another note you get a mode: from D dorian, from E phrygian, from F lydian, from G mixolydian, from A aeolian (natural minor) and from B locrian.

Each mode has a signature note. Dorian is minor with a major sixth (funk, Santana). Phrygian, minor with a minor second (flamenco, metal). Lydian, major with a raised fourth (dreamy, soundtracks). Mixolydian, major with a minor seventh (rock, blues, country).

To hear them, play the mode over a static chord on its tonic: the signature note stands out. The explorer marks it in another color.
lessonBodies(map).harmony:
If you build a chord on each note of the major scale using only scale notes you get seven chords: I major, ii minor, iii minor, IV major, V major, vi minor and vii diminished. In C: C Dm Em F G Am B°.

That list is the diatonic harmony and explains why certain chords sound good together: they belong to the same key. Roman numerals let you write progressions independent of key: 'I-V-vi-IV' is the same in C (C G Am F) as in G (G D Em C).

With four notes the jazz chords appear: Imaj7, ii7, iii7, IVmaj7, V7, vi7 and viiø. V7 is the only dominant: the one that asks to return to the tonic.
lessonBodies(map).degrees:
Each scale degree has a function. The tonic (I) is rest. The subdominant (IV) gently moves away. The dominant (V) builds tension and wants to resolve to the tonic.

The other degrees stand in for these three: vi and iii share notes with I (tonic function) and ii resembles IV (subdominant). That's why 'I-vi-IV-V' and 'I-IV-V' tell the same story: home, journey, tension and return.

Once you understand functions you can guess a song's next chord, figure out songs by ear and write your own progressions.
lessonBodies(map).progressions:
A progression is a repeating sequence of chords. A handful hold up much of popular music: I-V-vi-IV (pop), I-IV-V (rock, country, folk, ranchera), ii-V-I (jazz), vi-IV-I-V (ballads) and the Andalusian cadence i-bVII-bVI-V (flamenco and Latin rock).

Because they're written in degrees you can play them in any key: pick one that's comfortable to sing. Learn each progression in two or three keys and you'll start recognizing them everywhere.

The guided jam has all these progressions with backing, metronome, the strumming pattern and the recommended scale to improvise.
lessonBodies(map).caged:
The five open major chord shapes —C, A, G, E and D (C-A-G-E-D)— can move up the neck with a barre. Chained in that order they cover all twelve frets with the same chord.

For example, C major can be played as a C shape (open), an A shape (barre at fret 3), a G shape (fret 5), an E shape (fret 8) and a D shape (fret 10). Each shape shares notes with the next.

Each CAGED shape matches a major pentatonic box. That's how chords and scales connect: you always know which solo notes surround the chord you're playing.

lessonPoints(map).intervalSongs:
Interval = distance in semitones between two notes
m2 = "Jaws" · M2 = "Frère Jacques" · M3 = "When the Saints"
Perfect 4th = "Amazing Grace" · perfect 5th = "Twinkle Twinkle"
Tritone (6) = "Maria"; the most unstable one
Sing the interval before playing it, then check
lessonPoints(map).subdivision:
Quarters = beat · eighths = "1 and 2 and" · sixteenths = "1 e and a"
Triplet = three notes in one beat (slow blues, 6/8)
Syncopation = accent on the offbeat or silence on the beat
Swing/shuffle: a long + a short eighth (2 to 1)
Keep the arm always moving: down on the beat, up on the "and"
lessonPoints(map).modesPractical:
Dorian = minor 7 · major sixth (funk, jazz)
Mixolydian = dominant 7 · b7 (rock, blues, country)
Lydian = major maj7 · #4 (dreamy sound)
Phrygian = minor with b2 (flamenco, metal)
Play the characteristic note and resolve it to the tonic
lessonPoints(map).triads:
Major third = 4 semitones · minor third = 3
Major 0-4-7 · minor 0-3-7 · diminished 0-3-6 · augmented 0-4-8
Sevenths: maj7 (0-4-7-11) · 7 (0-4-7-10) · m7 (0-3-7-10)
The third decides whether it sounds happy or sad
In a major key: 3 major, 3 minor and 1 diminished chord
lessonPoints(map).extensions:
9 = 2nd up · 11 = 4th · 13 = 6th (an octave higher)
C9 = C7 + ninth: funk, soul, r&b
sus2 and sus4 replace the third; sus4 usually resolves to major
add9 = triad + ninth, no seventh (indie, pop)
Swap a chord for its colorful version and compare
lessonPoints(map).inversions:
First inversion = third in the bass · second = fifth
C/E = a C chord with E in the bass (the note after the slash)
A bass moving by step sounds fluid
C/E, G/B and D/F♯ are the most useful slash chords on guitar
Find the inversion shapes on each chord page
lessonPoints(map).circleFifths:
Right = +1 sharp per step · left = +1 flat
Circle neighbors share 6 of 7 notes
I with its IV (left) and V (right) = the three basic chords
Every major key holds its relative minor
Descending fifths: iii–vi–ii–V–I (jazz, ranchera, classic pop)
lessonPoints(map).cadences:
Authentic V–I (V7–I): the full stop
Plagal IV–I: the "amen", softer
Half cadence (ends on V): a comma, stays open
Deceptive V–vi: you expect I and get vi
Andalusian i–♭VII–♭VI–V (Am–G–F–E): flamenco and rumba
lessonPoints(map).relativeParallel:
Relative: same notes, different tonic (C ↔ A minor)
The relative minor is 3 semitones below the major tonic
Parallel: same tonic, different mode (C ↔ C minor)
Modal interchange: IV → iv, ♭VII, ♭VI come from the parallel key
If a song suddenly darkens, look for the borrowed chord
lessonPoints(map).transposeCapo:
Transposing = the same degrees in another key
Capo on fret N: raises everything by N semitones
Sounding key = shape + fret (G + 2 = A, C + 2 = D, D + 2 = E)
Pick open shapes (G, C, D, Em, Am) and work out the fret
The songbook transposes ±6 semitones
lessonPoints(map).styleComping:
Four ingredients: pattern, dynamics, register and muting
Pop: ↓ ↓↑ ↑↓↑ · reggae: only the offbeat
Ballad: arpeggio or one strum per bar
Cumbia: bass on 1 and 3 and a "chiqui" · funk: almost all muted
Play the same loop in four styles and compare
lessonPoints(map).tunings:
Standard = EADGBE
Drop D = DADGBE: one-finger power chords, heavy low end
DADGAD = open chords with no third (folk, fingerstyle)
Open G = DGDGBD: one finger or a slide makes the chords (blues)
Tune string by string and lower the pitch slowly
lessonPoints(map).notes:
12 notes: 7 natural and 5 sharps/flats
1 fret = 1 half step; 2 frets = 1 whole step
E–F and B–C are a half step apart
Fret 12 = the same note an octave up
Learn the notes on the 6th and 5th strings first: they are your barre-chord roots
lessonPoints(map).intervals:
Minor third = 3 half steps (sad)
Major third = 4 half steps (happy)
Perfect fifth = 7 half steps (power chord)
Octave = 12 half steps: the same note higher
The B string shifts shapes by one fret
lessonPoints(map).tonic:
Tonic = rest; moving away = tension
Key = tonic + scale
The last chord is usually the tonic
Every major key has a relative minor with the same notes
Transposing = moving everything by the same number of frets
lessonPoints(map).rhythm:
4/4: count 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and
3/4: count 1 and 2 and 3 and
The hand never stops: down on the beat, up on the 'and'
Start slow with a metronome and raise the tempo gradually
Change chords on the last stroke of the bar
lessonPoints(map).majorScale:
Formula: W W H W W W H (2-2-1-2-2-2-1 frets)
Seven notes, one of each letter
Its degrees are numbered 1 to 7
The key's chords come from it
It has 7 three-notes-per-string positions
lessonPoints(map).minorScales:
Natural minor: W H W W H W W
Relative minor = 3 half steps below the major
Same notes, different tonic
Harmonic minor: raised seventh
A major V in minor gives the flamenco cadence
lessonPoints(map).pentatonic:
Minor: 1 b3 4 5 b7
Major: 1 2 3 5 6
Two notes per string in each box
A minor pentatonic = C major pentatonic (same notes)
End your phrases on the tonic to sound resolved
lessonPoints(map).positions:
One box = 4-5 frets, one finger per fret
Pentatonic: 5 boxes; seven-note scales: 7 positions
Boxes overlap and repeat every 12 frets
Always locate the tonics inside the box
Moving the whole box = changing key
lessonPoints(map).blues:
Blues = minor pentatonic + b5
12 bars: I7 – IV7 – I7 – V7 – IV7 – I7
Every chord is a seventh chord
Shuffle: long-short on each beat
Bends and vibrato give it character
lessonPoints(map).modes:
Ionian = major · Aeolian = natural minor
Dorian: minor with a major 6th
Phrygian: minor with b2
Lydian: major with #4
Mixolydian: major with b7
lessonPoints(map).harmony:
Uppercase = major · lowercase = minor
In major: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
In minor: i ii° III iv v VI VII
Roman numerals = progressions in any key
V7 pulls toward I
lessonPoints(map).degrees:
I tonic: rest
IV subdominant: motion
V dominant: tension that returns to I
vi and iii act as tonic; ii as subdominant
V → I is the strongest cadence
lessonPoints(map).progressions:
Pop: I – V – vi – IV
Rock and country: I – IV – V
Jazz: ii – V – I
Ballad: vi – IV – I – V
Andalusian: i – bVII – bVI – V
lessonPoints(map).caged:
Order: C → A → G → E → D → C…
Each shape is a movable open chord
Together they cover the whole neck
Each shape sits on a pentatonic box
The root is always inside the shape
